demonstrations.title: How steady is an average when the guessers share a lean?
demonstrations.question: If each guesser's error has variance 1 and any two errors correlate, how much does the panel's average still vary, and what do extra guessers stop being able to fix?

symbols_list.meaning: the number of estimates, at least one
the common error variance of one member (set to 1 here)
the error correlation between any two members, taken as the same for every pair
how much the average varies across repeated panels

demonstrations.source_section: In an invented ledger, a small shared lean makes 787 guesses worth only 45
demonstrations.provenance: Book formula. The panel of four with correlation 0.2 giving 0.4 against 0.25 is the chapter's constructed example. The histogram is a seeded simulation (4000 panels) built to have exactly the stated correlation; it checks the formula and is not a measurement of any crowd.
demonstrations.assumptions: Equal weights, equal error variance, one pairwise correlation for all pairs, and no shared bias. The formula is about variance only: a lean that every member shares in the same direction is an extra problem it does not count.
demonstrations.prediction: With 4 guessers whose errors correlate at 0.2, predict whether the average's error variance is nearer 0.25 (unrelated errors) or 0.2 (the floor) before moving the sliders.

reveal.text: The average's error variance is 0.4: the unshared part, 0.8 divided by 4, is 0.2, and the shared part adds 0.2 more. With unrelated errors it would be 0.25. Slide n up: the curve flattens at 0.2, the floor.

demonstrations.takeaway: Averaging removes only the part of the error that guessers do not share; the shared part survives any headcount.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A panel that looks large can behave like a small one. Knowing the floor tells you when to stop adding look-alike members and look for a different source.

sides.brain: Nerve cells that respond to the same thing share some of their random noise, and a 1994 study reported a weak average correlation of 0.12 between pairs. The formula is a way to think about what that does to a pool; it is a model, and the study was not about judgment.
sides.machine: An ensemble average can be computed exactly given error variances and a correlation. The correlation of real models' errors still has to be measured, and the chapter says none of the studies did that.

demonstrations.explanation: Split each guesser's error into a part shared by everyone and a private part. Averaging cancels the private parts as the panel grows, so their contribution shrinks as one over n. The shared part is the same in every guess, so averaging leaves it untouched. The variance of the average is the sum of the two surviving pieces.
demonstrations.check: With 4 guessers and correlation 0.5, what is the error variance of the average, and what is the floor?
demonstrations.answer: (1 - 0.5)/4 + 0.5 = 0.125 + 0.5 = 0.625. The floor is the correlation itself, 0.5. Unrelated errors would give 0.25.
demonstrations.alt: Histogram of simulated panel averages with bell curves, and variance of the average against panel size for four correlations.
demonstrations.symbols: n: the number of estimates, at least one; sigma^2: the common error variance of one member (set to 1 here); rho: the error correlation between any two members, taken as the same for every pair; Var(X-bar): how much the average varies across repeated panels
demonstrations.application: A panel that looks large can behave like a small one. Knowing the floor tells you when to stop adding look-alike members and look for a different source.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: With 4 guessers, each with error variance 1 and pairwise error correlation 0.2, the average has error variance 0.4, against 0.25 if the errors were unrelated. Adding guessers can never take it below 0.2.

demonstrations.title: How many independent guessers is a crowd worth?
demonstrations.question: If 787 guessers share a small error correlation of 0.021, how many independent guessers do they equal, and what happens when a thousand more join?

symbols_list.meaning: the number of guessers
the error correlation between any two guessers; here a chosen value
effective panel size: how many independent guessers give an average as steady as the panel's
the ceiling the effective size approaches as the panel grows; undefined when rho is 0

demonstrations.source_section: In an invented ledger, a small shared lean makes 787 guesses worth only 45
demonstrations.provenance: Book formula. The 787 guessers are Galton's count, but the correlation 0.021 is chosen by the chapter and nothing about Galton's guessers supports it. The values 0.05 and 0.12 are added here for contrast; 0.12 is the weak average correlation between pairs of nerve cells that a 1994 study reported, used as an idealization with every pair equal.
demonstrations.assumptions: Equal error variance, one correlation for every pair, equal weights. The effective size counts steadiness only. It is not a measure of shared bias or of how many distinct opinions there are.
demonstrations.prediction: With correlation 0.021, predict the effective size of 787 guessers, and whether adding a thousand more would roughly double it.

reveal.text: 787 guessers are worth 45.0, about 45. Switch n to 1787 and the worth only rises to 46.4, because the ceiling is 1/0.021, about 48.

demonstrations.takeaway: A large panel with even a small shared error is worth far fewer heads than its count, and the worth stalls at 1 divided by the correlation.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: Headcounts and ensemble sizes overstate what a pool knows when members share influences. Estimating how much their mistakes overlap is the number that matters.

sides.brain: A 1994 study reported weak correlated noise between pairs of cells, averaging 0.12, and argued it can limit what a pool can signal; a 2020 study reported correlated noise limiting signalling in groups of 800 to 1,300 mouse visual cells. Applying one equal correlation to every pair is an idealization, not what those studies fitted.
sides.machine: For an ensemble, the formula turns a stated error correlation into a worth. The correlation of real models' errors is not supplied by any study in the chapter.

demonstrations.explanation: The variance of an average is sigma squared times (1 - rho)/n plus rho. An average of n independent guessers has variance sigma squared over n, so setting the two equal gives n_eff. As n grows, the first piece vanishes and only the floor rho remains, so the worth cannot exceed 1 over rho.
demonstrations.check: Using n = 100 and correlation 0.05, what is the effective size, and what is the ceiling?
demonstrations.alt: Effective panel size against number of guessers with the ceiling 1 over rho, and worth per head against panel size for four correlations.
demonstrations.symbols: n: the number of guessers; rho: the error correlation between any two guessers; here a chosen value; n_eff: effective panel size: how many independent guessers give an average as steady as the panel's; 1/rho: the ceiling the effective size approaches as the panel grows; undefined when rho is 0
demonstrations.application: Headcounts and ensemble sizes overstate what a pool knows when members share influences. Estimating how much their mistakes overlap is the number that matters.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: 787 guessers whose errors correlate at 0.021 are worth 45 independent ones, or 0.0571 of a head each. No panel of this kind can be worth more than 47.6.

demonstrations.title: Which average survives a few wildly wrong guesses?
demonstrations.question: When a few guesses are off by a whole size class, how far does the plain average move compared with the median and the geometric mean?

symbols_list.meaning: guess number i, positive
the number of guesses (144 here)
the geometric mean: the plain average of the logs, turned back into a count

demonstrations.source_section: Guessing Swiss murders, alone and in sight of others
demonstrations.provenance: Constructed sample, not the students' data. The question (198 murders registered in Switzerland in 2006) and the group of 144 follow the chapter's account of Lorenz and colleagues, who reported a mean of 838, a median of 170 and a geometric mean of about 174 on first guesses. Here 144 guesses are drawn with seed 2011 around 190, and some are multiplied by 10, 100 or 1000 to imitate a wrong size class.
demonstrations.assumptions: The bulk of guesses is unbiased in logs and the outliers are a pure multiple of the bulk. Real guesses will not split so cleanly. Which average is best depends on the shape of the errors, and no rule is best for all shapes.
demonstrations.prediction: If 5 percent of 144 guesses are 100 times too large, predict whether the arithmetic mean ends up within 20 percent of the true count or several times above it.

reveal.text: Seven guesses 100 times too large lift the arithmetic mean from 242 to 1181, about 6.0 times the true 198, while the geometric mean moves only from 197 to 246 and the median from 198 to 220.

demonstrations.takeaway: One long tail of guesses in the wrong size class drags a plain average up without limit, while a median and a geometric mean react far less.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: Pooling rules are decisions about the shape of the errors. A machine applies any rule exactly the same way each time, so choosing the rule is the part a person still owns.
demonstrations.explanation: A plain average adds the guesses, so a single guess a thousand times too big contributes a thousand times too much. The median looks only at the middle guess, so it changes only if the outliers cross the middle. The geometric mean averages the logs, so a factor of 100 adds only the log of 100 to one term.
demonstrations.check: In a group of 4 guesses 100, 100, 100 and 10,000, what are the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean?

controls.label: Share of guesses in the wrong size class
How far off those guesses are (times)

demonstrations.alt: Dot chart of the arithmetic mean, geometric mean and median against the true count, and mean over truth against the share of outliers.
demonstrations.symbols: x_i: guess number i, positive; n: the number of guesses (144 here); g-bar: the geometric mean: the plain average of the logs, turned back into a count
demonstrations.application: Pooling rules are decisions about the shape of the errors. A machine applies any rule exactly the same way each time, so choosing the rule is the part a person still owns.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Share of guesses in the wrong size class: 0.05 · How far off those guesses are (times): 100
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: With 7 of 144 constructed guesses multiplied by 100, the arithmetic mean is 1181, 5.96 times the true 198. The geometric mean, 246.3, and the median, 219.7, move much less.

demonstrations.title: Why can social influence narrow a crowd without making it more right?
demonstrations.question: If every member moves part of the way to the crowd's average, what happens to the crowd's own error and to the members' average error?

symbols_list.meaning: member i's guess on the log scale
the crowd average of the logs, which is the geometric mean on the original scale
the true value on the log scale
the number of members (12 here)

demonstrations.source_section: Guessing Swiss murders, alone and in sight of others
demonstrations.provenance: Book identity (stated on logs). The 12 guesses are constructed with seed 2012 (a low lean of 0.25 in log10 units and spread 0.4), and the pull rule is the chapter's simple model of moving the same part of the way to the crowd average. The chapter says the study did not fit this rule to the students.
demonstrations.assumptions: Every member moves the same fraction toward the current crowd average each round. The study found that guesses grew more alike and the crowd's error did not fall significantly in its main test. This computation shows why those can go together; it does not fit the students' revisions.
demonstrations.prediction: If every member moves half the way to the crowd average three times, predict whether the crowd's own squared miss changes and by what factor the disagreement shrinks.

reveal.text: The crowd's squared miss stays put while the average individual squared miss falls from 0.189 to 0.045, because disagreement shrinks by a factor of (0.5)^6, about 0.0156.

demonstrations.takeaway: The members' average miss splits into the crowd's own miss plus their disagreement. Pulling toward the average removes only the disagreement.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A group that becomes more alike can look more accurate member by member while knowing exactly as much as before. Diversity is what pooling uses, and influence uses it up.
demonstrations.explanation: Average squared miss equals the squared miss of the crowd average plus the average squared distance of members from that average. Moving each member a fixed fraction toward the average leaves the average where it was and scales every distance from it by one minus the fraction. So the second piece shrinks while the first stays.
demonstrations.check: Two guesses on the log scale are 1 and 3, and the truth is 3. They each move halfway to their average once. What are the average squared miss before and after?
demonstrations.answer: Before: (4 + 0)/2 = 2. The average is 2, so after one round they sit at 1.5 and 2.5, giving (2.25 + 0.25)/2 = 1.25. The crowd's own squared miss is (2 - 3)^2 = 1 both times, and the disagreement falls from 1 to 0.25.

controls.label: Fraction moved toward the crowd each round

demonstrations.alt: Twelve constructed guesses before and after pulling toward the group, and average squared miss against pull for 1, 3 and 5 rounds.
demonstrations.symbols: y_i: member i's guess on the log scale; y-bar: the crowd average of the logs, which is the geometric mean on the original scale; t: the true value on the log scale; n: the number of members (12 here)
demonstrations.application: A group that becomes more alike can look more accurate member by member while knowing exactly as much as before. Diversity is what pooling uses, and influence uses it up.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Fraction moved toward the crowd each round: 0.5 · Rounds of influence: 3
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: Each of 12 constructed guessers moves 0.5 of the way to the group's log average, 3 time(s). The average squared miss falls from 0.189 to 0.0452, while the crowd's own squared miss stays 0.0429.

demonstrations.title: What does an independent check add that a tenth look-alike cannot?
demonstrations.question: For nine models with error variance 1 and error correlation 0.4, what does a tenth similar model buy, and what does an independent check buy?

symbols_list.meaning: the number of models in the panel
the error correlation between any two panel members, chosen here
error variance of the panel's average, each member having variance 1
error variance of an unbiased check whose errors are unrelated to the panel's

demonstrations.source_section: Two heads in a contrast test: similar partners gained, very unequal pairs could lose
demonstrations.provenance: Chapter's constructed example (nine models, variance 1, correlation 0.4, giving about 0.47, then about 0.32 with a check), computed here with extra panel sizes and correlations. The numbers are invented, as the chapter says.
demonstrations.assumptions: All estimates are unbiased for the same quantity, the check's errors are independent of the panel's, and the weights use the true variances. If the check shares the panel's sources or any source is biased, the combined variance is not what the formula gives.
demonstrations.prediction: Before moving the sliders, predict whether a tenth model like the other nine lowers the panel's variance by more or less than one percent of a unit.

reveal.text: The panel of nine has variance 0.467 and a tenth member only 0.46, a gain of 0.007. An independent check of variance 1, weighted by precision, takes it to 0.318.

demonstrations.takeaway: Once members share error, the next look-alike barely helps, while one source with independent errors can help a lot even if it is individually no better.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: The useful question for a partnership is where each answer came from, not only how reliable it seems. A source that fails for different reasons is worth more than another copy of the same reason.

sides.brain: In Bahrami and colleagues' 2010 contrast-test pairs, partners with similar sensitivity beat their better member, and very unequal pairs could lose. The model that fit was weighted confidence sharing, and the pairs pooled less well than an ideal inverse-variance rule would. Those are behavioral results from 15 pairs in the first experiment.
sides.machine: An ensemble plus a verifier can be combined by inverse-variance weighting if the verifier's errors are independent of the ensemble's. The chapter's nine models and their variances are invented.

demonstrations.explanation: The panel average cannot fall below the shared error rho, so adding a similar member moves it only a little. An independent source has no part in that shared error, so combining by precision (one over variance) pulls the answer below the floor of the panel alone. The combined precision is the sum of the two precisions.
demonstrations.check: A panel has variance 0.5 and an independent check has variance 0.5. What is the combined variance?
demonstrations.answer: Precisions are 2 and 2, which add to 4, so the variance is 1/4 = 0.25.

controls.label: Error variance of the independent check

demonstrations.alt: Bars of error variance for a panel, a bigger panel, a check and the panel plus check, and panel variance against size for three correlations.
demonstrations.symbols: n: the number of models in the panel; rho: the error correlation between any two panel members, chosen here; V_panel: error variance of the panel's average, each member having variance 1; V_check: error variance of an unbiased check whose errors are unrelated to the panel's
demonstrations.application: The useful question for a partnership is where each answer came from, not only how reliable it seems. A source that fails for different reasons is worth more than another copy of the same reason.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Models in the panel: 9 · Error correlation among them: 0.4 · Error variance of the independent check: 1.0
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: A panel of 9 with error variance 1 and correlation 0.4 averages to variance 0.467, and a panel of 10 only to 0.46. An independent check of variance 1, weighted by precision, takes it to 0.318.

demonstrations.title: Can independent models agree on a wrong answer by temptation alone?
demonstrations.question: If two models never see each other's answers but one wrong option tempts both, how often do they pick the same wrong option?

symbols_list.meaning: model 1's chance of choosing wrong option j, given it is wrong
model 2's chance of choosing wrong option j, given it is wrong
the share of wrong answers going to the most tempting option; the other two options share the rest equally

demonstrations.source_section: Models that pick the same wrong option
demonstrations.provenance: Constructed illustration. The reported figures are from Kim and colleagues as the chapter gives them: an average match of 0.6 over pairs among 71 models on questions both got wrong, against 1/3 for uniform random choice among three wrong options. The shape of the wrong-option shares here is invented to show a mechanism, not fitted to their data.
demonstrations.assumptions: Both models choose independently and each has the same fixed shares over three wrong options. The chapter notes that some wrong options look closer to right and would draw independent models too, so the gap above 1/3 does not by itself measure excess agreement. The 0.6 is an average over pairs, not an error correlation.
demonstrations.prediction: If the single most tempting wrong option draws 60 percent of each model's wrong answers, predict whether independent models would match about 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6 of the time.

reveal.text: With 0.6 of wrong answers on one shared option, independent models match 0.6 x 0.6 + 2 x 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.44 of the time, well above 1/3 and still below the reported 0.6. It takes a share of about 0.755 to reach 0.6.

demonstrations.takeaway: Agreement on wrong options is not proof that models copy each other: shared temptation produces it with no communication.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: Voting and averaging assume independence. Matching on wrong answers is a warning for that assumption, but this figure cannot be dropped into the error-correlation formula, and why it arises is not established.

sides.machine: The study compared 71 models on a public leaderboard and found higher matching for models from the same developer and for larger, more accurate ones. The chapter says why this happens is not established.

demonstrations.explanation: Two independent choosers match when both land on the same option. Their match chance is the sum, over options, of the product of the two shares. With uniform shares over three options this is 3 times (1/3)^2 = 1/3. Concentrating the shares on one option raises the sum. If the two models are tempted by different options, the sum is smaller.
demonstrations.check: If 0.5 of each model's wrong answers go to the same option and the other two share the rest, what is the match chance?

controls.label: Share of wrong answers on the most tempting option
Which option tempts the second model

demonstrations.alt: Bars of two models' shares over three wrong options, and chance of matching against the share on the most tempting option.
demonstrations.symbols: p_j: model 1's chance of choosing wrong option j, given it is wrong; q_j: model 2's chance of choosing wrong option j, given it is wrong; L: the share of wrong answers going to the most tempting option; the other two options share the rest equally
demonstrations.application: Voting and averaging assume independence. Matching on wrong answers is a warning for that assumption, but this figure cannot be dropped into the error-correlation formula, and why it arises is not established.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Share of wrong answers on the most tempting option: 0.34 · Which option tempts the second model: same wrong option
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: If independent models send 0.34 of their wrong answers to their most tempting option, and the same option tempts both models, they match 0.333 of the time. Reaching the reported 0.6 this way takes a share of 0.755 on one shared option.

demonstrations.title: When does a majority vote over sampled answers help?
demonstrations.question: If a model samples many chains of reasoning and the most common answer wins, when does the vote beat one chain, and when does it make things worse?

symbols_list.meaning: the number of sampled chains, odd so there are no ties
the chance one chain is right on this question
how many of the m chains are right

demonstrations.source_section: Models that pick the same wrong option
demonstrations.provenance: Constructed population, not a result. Easy questions (60 percent of them) have chain accuracy 0.8 and hard ones a chosen lower value. The chapter reports, for PaLM-540B on grade-school math, 56.5 percent with one chain and 74.4 percent with a vote over 40 chains (mean of 10 runs), and 36.9 percent when PaLM-540B and a smaller model voted together; this demonstration does not reproduce those figures.
demonstrations.assumptions: Chains are drawn independently given the question, each right with a fixed chance for that question, and wrong chains are treated as not forming a majority for the right answer. In real use all chains share one model's strengths and biases and wrong chains may agree with each other.
demonstrations.prediction: If a hard question has a chain chance of 0.3, predict whether a vote of 41 chains on it is right more often or less often than one chain.

reveal.text: On hard questions a vote of 41 is right only 0.004 of the time, against 0.3 for one chain, while easy questions rise to 1.000. Overall the vote scores 0.601 against 0.60 for one chain. With hard-question chance 0.45 the vote scores 0.704 against 0.660.

demonstrations.takeaway: A vote pushes each question toward certainty in whichever direction a single chain already leans, so it helps only where chains are right more often than not.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: Adding votes does not repair a model that gives the same wrong answer most of the time. The chapter's cross-model vote did worse than the best single model because lower-capacity models dragged it down.

sides.machine: Self-consistency samples several chains from one model and takes the most common final answer. The chains are independent draws for a given question yet still share that model's strengths and biases.

demonstrations.explanation: For one question with chain chance p, the vote is right when more than half of the chains are. For p above one half the chance climbs toward 1 as chains are added, and for p below one half it falls toward 0. The overall effect is the average across questions, so it depends on how many questions lean each way.
demonstrations.check: With p = 0.6 on a question, what is the chance that a vote of 3 chains is right?
demonstrations.answer: Right when at least 2 of 3 chains are right: 3 x 0.6^2 x 0.4 + 0.6^3 = 0.432 + 0.216 = 0.648.

controls.label: Chance one chain is right on a hard question

demonstrations.alt: Bars of one chain against a vote on easy, hard and all questions, and overall accuracy against the number of chains for four hard-question chances.
demonstrations.symbols: m: the number of sampled chains, odd so there are no ties; p: the chance one chain is right on this question; k: how many of the m chains are right
demonstrations.application: Adding votes does not repair a model that gives the same wrong answer most of the time. The chapter's cross-model vote did worse than the best single model because lower-capacity models dragged it down.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Chains voting: 11 · Chance one chain is right on a hard question: 0.3
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: In a constructed mix with 60 percent easy questions (each chain right with chance 0.8) and hard ones (chance 0.3), one chain scores 0.6 and a vote of 11 scores 0.624. Voting lifts easy questions toward certainty and sinks hard ones.
